summary: "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour," a concert film made through a direct deal with AMC Theaters that bypasses Hollywood studios, has passed $100 million in worldwide advance sales and is expected to open with $100 million or more. The article describes how theaters are preparing for fan-driven screenings, and how the deal, along with Beyoncé's similar one, may open movie theaters to new kinds of content and business models. Analysts and an ex-DOJ antitrust chief see the end of the Paramount consent decrees and industry upheaval as enabling this experimentation.
one_line: Taylor Swift's Eras Tour concert film, distributed directly through AMC, has topped $100 million in advance sales and could reshape how theaters and studios do business.
key_facts: "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" debuts on a Friday in October 2023 and is expected to open with $100 million, possibly more; worldwide advance ticket sales have already surpassed $100 million.
The concert film was compiled from several Swift shows at Southern California's SoFi Stadium and directed by Sam Wrench.
Adult tickets cost $19.89, a reference to Swift's birth year and her 2014 album, a re-recording of which is due out Oct. 27.
Ticket revenue is split 43% to theaters and 57% shared by Swift and AMC, with the lion's share going to Swift.
The film will play exclusively in theaters for at least 13 weeks, longer than many Hollywood releases.
Beyoncé is set to release a concert film in December under a very similar direct arrangement with AMC Theaters.
Pollstar projects the Eras Tour to gross some $1.4 billion; it crashed Ticketmaster's site and saw sky-high resale mark-ups.
There are no advance screenings after the Los Angeles premiere on Wednesday; the film begins playing at 6 p.m. local time Friday.
TV ads for the film ran only a few dozen times as of Oct. 6, per iSpot, compared with several thousand for a typical Marvel movie; Swift has 274 million Instagram followers.
Comscore's Paul Dergarabedian believes the two concert films could lift 2023 North American box office to more than $9 billion, up from $7.4 billion in 2022 and closer to $11.4 billion in 2019.
The Paramount consent decrees, in place more than 70 years, were terminated in 2020 at the urging of the Department of Justice, with a two-year sunset period that ran until 2022.
The current biggest concert film is 2011's "Justin Bieber: Never Say Never" with $73.1 million; "Woodstock" grossed $50 million in 1970, nearly $400 million today.
Marcus Corporation theaters will have friendship bracelet stations and sound systems modified for a concert feel.
